subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 2! In this unit you will become a confident expert on two-dimensional shapes – the flat shapes that live all around you. A 2D shape is any shape that is flat, with only length and width and no thickness, like a picture drawn on paper. You will meet polygons, learn to sort triangles and quadrilaterals by their sides and angles, discover the two kinds of symmetry, and explore how shapes fit together in tessellations and repeating patterns.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

provenance.transformation: Structured from the Cambridge Primary Mathematics 0096 — Stage 5 workbook source documents for screen presentation.

outcomes: Identify and name polygons by their number of sides, and tell regular from irregular polygons.
Describe a shape using the correct language of sides, vertices (corners) and angles.
Classify triangles by their sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by their angles (right, acute, obtuse).
Classify quadrilaterals (square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium, kite) by their properties.
Find all the lines of symmetry in a 2D shape and understand line (reflective) symmetry.
Understand rotational symmetry and state the order of rotational symmetry of a shape.
Explain what a tessellation is and why some shapes tessellate while others leave gaps.
Recognise, describe and continue repeating geometric patterns.
Identify perpendicular lines (crossing at a right angle) and parallel lines (running in the same direction and never meeting) in shapes and in everyday objects.
Create and complete patterns that have two lines of symmetry, such as a design reflected in both a vertical and a horizontal mirror line on a square grid.

concepts.title: Polygons and the Language of Shape
concepts.explanation:
A polygon is a flat, closed shape made only of straight sides. The word comes from two old Greek words: *poly* meaning ‘many’ and *gon* meaning ‘angle’, so a polygon is literally a ‘many-angled’ shape. To be a polygon, a shape must obey three rules: it must be closed (the sides join all the way round with no gaps), it must have only straight sides (no curves), and the sides must not cross over each other.

This means a circle is not a polygon, because its edge is curved. A shape with a gap in its outline is not a polygon either, because it is not closed. But a triangle, a square, a pentagon and a hexagon are all proud members of the polygon family.

We name polygons by counting their sides. Learning these names is like learning the names of a big family – once you know them, you can talk about any flat shape with confidence:

Notice a lovely fact in that table: the number of sides always equals the number of vertices. This is true for every polygon. A hexagon has 6 sides and 6 corners; a decagon has 10 sides and 10 corners. Each time one side ends, another begins at a vertex, so they always come in matching pairs.

To describe any shape well, you need three key words. A side (also called an edge) is one of the straight lines that make the boundary. A vertex is a corner, the point where two sides meet – and when we talk about more than one, we say vertices. An angle is the amount of turning at a vertex, measured in degrees. When Farah describes the triangular sign on the road to Berbera, she can now say precisely: ‘It is a polygon with three sides, three vertices and three angles.’
concepts.example: Polygons come in two important kinds. A regular polygon has all its sides the same length AND all its angles the same size. A regular triangle is the equilateral triangle; a regular quadrilateral is the square. An irregular polygon has sides or angles that are not all equal – for example a long thin rectangle, or a triangle with three different side lengths. Do not be fooled: a shape can have equal sides but still be irregular if its angles are not equal, and the other way round. To be *regular*, a polygon must be equal in both ways at once.

concepts.title: Classifying Triangles by Their Sides
concepts.explanation:
The triangle is the simplest polygon of all, and one of the most important shapes in the world. It has 3 sides, 3 vertices and 3 angles. Triangles appear everywhere in building and engineering because they are extremely strong and rigid – push on a triangle and it holds its shape, which is why you see triangular braces in roofs, bridges, cranes and market-stall frames.

There are two completely different ways to sort triangles: by their sides and by their angles. We will learn both, because a full description often uses both together. First, sorting by sides. There are three types:

Equilateral triangle – all three sides are equal, and all three angles are equal too (each is exactly 60°). This is the *regular* triangle.

Isosceles triangle – exactly two sides are equal, and the two angles opposite those equal sides are equal too.

Scalene triangle – no sides are equal and no angles are equal. Every side and every angle is different.

The names sound difficult, but they have friendly meanings. *Equilateral* breaks into *equi* (equal) and *lateral* (sides), so it means ‘equal sides’. *Isosceles* comes from words meaning ‘equal legs’ – picture a triangle standing on two matching legs. *Scalene* means ‘uneven’. Say each word a few times and it will stick.

Here is a useful rule that links sides to angles: equal sides always sit opposite equal angles. In an isosceles triangle, the two equal sides push the two base angles to be equal. In an equilateral triangle, all three sides are equal, so all three angles must be equal too – and because the angles of any triangle always add up to 180°, each angle is 180° ÷ 3 = 60°. This is why you can identify an equilateral triangle either by its equal sides or by its three 60° angles.

Worked Example: Identifying a triangle by its sides

Hassan measures a triangular scarf and finds its sides are 5 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm. What type is it?

Step 1: Are all three sides equal? No – 5, 5 and 8 are not all the same, so it is not equilateral.

Step 2: Are exactly two sides equal? Yes – two sides are 5 cm.
concepts.example: Answer: It is an isosceles triangle, because it has exactly two equal sides. We would also expect its two base angles (opposite the 5 cm sides) to be equal.

concepts.title: Classifying Triangles by Their Angles
concepts.explanation:
Using angles, there are three types of triangle:

Right-angled triangle – has one angle that is exactly 90° (a right angle). You see these in set squares and in the corner of a roof brace.

Acute triangle – all three angles are less than 90°. Every corner is a small, sharp angle.

Obtuse triangle – has one angle greater than 90° (one blunt, wide-open corner). A triangle can have only one obtuse angle.

Why can a triangle have only one right angle or only one obtuse angle? Because the three angles of any triangle always add up to exactly 180°. This is one of the most important facts in all of geometry. If one angle were 90° and another were also 90°, they would already use up all 180°, leaving nothing for the third angle – which is impossible. So a triangle can have at most one right angle and at most one obtuse angle.

The clever part is that the two ways of sorting can be combined. A triangle can be *both* isosceles *and* right-angled at the same time – like a set square with two equal short sides and one right angle. It can be scalene and obtuse, or isosceles and acute. A full, expert description uses both words: for example, ‘a right-angled scalene triangle’ or ‘an acute isosceles triangle’. When Khadija describes a shape completely, she names the side-type and the angle-type together.

A triangle has two angles measuring 60° and 70°. What is the third angle, and what type of triangle is it by its angles?

Step 1: Add the two known angles: 60° + 70° = 130°.

Step 2: Subtract from 180° to find the missing angle: 180° − 130° = 50°.

Step 3: Look at all three angles: 60°, 70° and 50°. Every one is less than 90°, so all are acute.
concepts.example: Answer: The third angle is 50°, and the triangle is an acute triangle because all three of its angles are acute.

concepts.title: Classifying Quadrilaterals
concepts.explanation:
A quadrilateral is any polygon with 4 sides, 4 vertices and 4 angles. The word breaks into *quad* (four) and *lateral* (sides). Just as with triangles, there is a whole family of special quadrilaterals, each with its own properties. Another vital fact: the four angles inside any quadrilateral always add up to 360° – a full turn. Here are the important members of the family:

4 lines of symmetry; the regular quadrilateral

Opposite sides equal; 4 right angles

4 equal sides; opposite angles equal

A 'pushed-over' square; 2 lines of symmetry

Opposite sides equal and parallel; no right angles needed

Two pairs of equal sides that are next to each other

Let us look more closely. A square is the most special of all: it has four equal sides and four right angles, so it is the *regular* quadrilateral. A rectangle keeps the four right angles but only its opposite sides are equal – picture a door or a prayer mat, longer than it is wide. Notice that every square is also a rectangle (it just happens to have all sides equal), but not every rectangle is a square.

A rhombus is like a square that has been gently pushed over: it still has four equal sides, but its angles are no longer right angles – two are acute and two are obtuse. A diamond shape in a woven basket is often a rhombus. A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides and opposite sides equal, but it leans over and has no right angles; think of a rectangle that has been slanted sideways.

A trapezium has exactly one pair of parallel sides – the two parallel sides are different lengths, like the sloping profile of a hillside terrace. A kite has two pairs of equal sides, but the equal sides are next to each other (adjacent) rather than opposite; it looks just like the flying kite children make from sticks and paper. Learning to spot which pairs of sides are equal and which are parallel is the key to naming any quadrilateral correctly.

These shapes are connected in a family tree. Because a square has everything a rectangle has (four right angles) and everything a rhombus has (four equal sides), a square is a special rectangle *and* a special rhombus at the same time. Thinking about how shapes belong to more than one group is a sign of real geometric understanding.

Worked Example: Naming a quadrilateral

Zahra draws a shape with four equal sides, but its angles are 70°, 110°, 70° and 110°. What is it?

Step 1: Four equal sides suggests a square or a rhombus.

Step 2: Are the angles all 90°? No – they are 70° and 110°, so it is not a square.

Step 3: Check the angle sum: 70 + 110 + 70 + 110 = 360°. Good, that is a valid quadrilateral.
concepts.example: Answer: It is a rhombus – four equal sides but no right angles.

concepts.title: Line (Reflective) Symmetry
concepts.explanation: Symmetry is one of the most beautiful ideas in mathematics, and you can see it in flowers, in butterflies, in the patterns on a woven mat, and in the careful designs on a masjid door. A shape has line symmetry (also called reflective or mirror symmetry) when you can fold it along a straight line so that both halves match exactly, with one half sitting perfectly on top of the other. That fold line is called a line of symmetry. The best way to test for a line of symmetry is the fold test: imagine folding the shape… You can also use symmetry to design a pattern that has two lines of symmetry at once, for example a horizontal line and a vertical line crossing in the middle of a square grid. Colour a small pattern of squares in just one quarter of the grid. To give the picture a vertical line of symmetry, reflect your quarter sideways into the next quarter, so each coloured square has a matching coloured square the same distance from the line on the other side. To also give the picture a horizontal line of symmetry, reflect the half you now have downward into the bottom half in the same way. The finished picture, covering all four quarters, will fold perfectly in half both up-and-down and side-to-side, which is exactly what having two lines of symmetry means.
concepts.example: Let us count the lines of symmetry for shapes you now know well: For instance, if you colour the square 2 across and 3 up in the bottom-left quarter of a 6-by-6 grid, a pattern with two lines of symmetry will also have a coloured square at the matching spot in each of the other three quarters.

concepts.title: Rotational Symmetry
concepts.explanation:
There is a second kind of symmetry that has nothing to do with folding. A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks exactly the same as you turn it around its centre point, before it has gone all the way round. Imagine pinning a shape at its centre and slowly spinning it: if at some point during a full turn it looks identical to how it started, it has rotational symmetry.

We measure rotational symmetry by its order – the number of times the shape looks the same during one complete turn (one full 360° rotation). To find the order, count how many different positions during a full turn look exactly like the starting position.

A square has rotational symmetry of order 4 – it looks the same after turning a quarter-turn (90°), a half-turn (180°), a three-quarter turn (270°) and a full turn.

An equilateral triangle has rotational symmetry of order 3 – it matches itself every 120° of turn.

A rectangle (that is not a square) has rotational symmetry of order 2 – it matches after a half-turn (180°) and a full turn.

A shape that only matches after a full turn has order 1, which we simply say has no rotational symmetry.

Here is a neat way to find the angle you must turn: divide 360° by the order. A square (order 4) matches every 360 ÷ 4 = 90°. An equilateral triangle (order 3) matches every 360 ÷ 3 = 120°. This connects rotation to division, showing again how the different parts of maths fit together.
concepts.example: Be careful not to confuse the two symmetries. Line symmetry is about *folding* (reflection). Rotational symmetry is about *turning*. A shape can have one, both, or neither. A square has plenty of both. A parallelogram has no line symmetry but does have rotational symmetry of order 2 – a lovely reminder that the two ideas are truly different.

concepts.title: Perpendicular and Parallel Lines
concepts.explanation: Two straight lines can relate to each other in special ways, and two of the most important are perpendicular and parallel. Lines are perpendicular when they cross at a right angle (exactly 90°) — think of the corner of a book, a window frame, or the letter T, where the upright and the crossbar meet squarely. You can test whether two lines are perpendicular by holding a right-angle tester, such as the corner of a piece of paper, against the crossing point: if it fits exactly with no gap on either side, the lines are perpendicular. Lines are parallel when they run in exactly the same direction and never meet, no matter how far they are extended in either direction — like the two rails of a railway track or the two long edges of a ruler. Parallel lines always stay the same distance apart. On a diagram, parallel lines are usually marked with small matching arrows (single arrows on one pair, double arrows on another pair if there is more than one set), and you already met this idea when you spotted the parallel sides of a rectangle, a parallelogram and a trapezium.
concepts.example: Look again at your quadrilaterals: a rectangle has two pairs of parallel sides, and every corner is also a pair of perpendicular sides meeting at 90°, so a rectangle shows both properties at once. A trapezium has only one pair of parallel sides. A kite has no parallel sides at all, but it does have one pair of perpendicular diagonals (the two lines connecting opposite corners cross at a right angle in the middle).

methods.title: How to classify a triangle
methods.example: A flat, closed shape has 6 straight, equal sides and 6 equal angles. Name it and say whether it is regular.
steps: Look at the sides: all equal = equilateral; two equal = isosceles; none equal = scalene.
Look at the angles: one 90° = right-angled; all under 90° = acute; one over 90° = obtuse.
Combine both words for a full description, for example ‘acute isosceles’.

methods.title: How to find lines of symmetry
methods.example: A triangle has sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 4 cm. Describe it fully.
steps: Imagine folding the shape along a line.
Check whether both halves land exactly on top of each other.
Count every fold line that works — that is the number of lines of symmetry.

methods.title: How to test for tessellation
methods.example: Two angles of a triangle are 90° and 55°. Find the third angle and classify the triangle by its angles.
steps: Find the angle of the shape that meets at each point.
Check whether copies of that angle can add up to exactly 360°.
If they can, the shape tessellates; if they leave a gap or overlap, it does not.

methods.title: Name the quadrilateral
methods.example: A shape has exactly one pair of parallel sides. What is it?
steps: Exactly one pair of parallel sides means it is a trapezium.
Count how many pairs of sides are parallel before naming the shape.
Check by looking for a second pair of parallel sides — if there isn't one, it stays a trapezium, not a parallelogram.

methods.title: Count lines of symmetry
methods.example: How many lines of symmetry does an isosceles triangle have, and where is it?
steps: An isosceles triangle has 1 line of symmetry.
It runs from the top vertex (between the two equal sides) straight down to the middle of the base, so the two equal sides fold onto each other.
Check by folding a paper triangle along your line — the two halves should match exactly.

methods.title: State the order of rotational symmetry
methods.example: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a rectangle that is not a square?
steps: Turn it around its centre.
It looks the same after a half-turn (180°) and after a full turn (360°) — two matching positions.
So the order is 2.

workedExamples.title: Name the polygon
workedExamples.prompt: A flat, closed shape has 6 straight, equal sides and 6 equal angles. Name it and say whether it is regular.
workedExamples.solution: Six sides means it is a hexagon. Because all sides are equal AND all angles are equal, it is a regular hexagon.

workedExamples.title: Classify by sides and angles
workedExamples.prompt: A triangle has sides 4 cm, 4 cm and 4 cm. Describe it fully.
workedExamples.solution: All three sides are equal, so by sides it is equilateral. In an equilateral triangle every angle is 60°, all acute, so by angles it is acute. Full description: an acute equilateral triangle (the regular triangle).

workedExamples.title: Use the 180° rule
workedExamples.prompt: Two angles of a triangle are 90° and 55°. Find the third angle and classify the triangle by its angles.
workedExamples.solution: 90 + 55 = 145. Then 180 − 145 = 35°. Because one angle is exactly 90°, it is a right-angled triangle.

workedExamples.title: Name the quadrilateral
workedExamples.prompt: A shape has exactly one pair of parallel sides. What is it?
workedExamples.solution: Exactly one pair of parallel sides means it is a trapezium.

workedExamples.title: Count lines of symmetry
workedExamples.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does an isosceles triangle have, and where is it?
workedExamples.solution: An isosceles triangle has 1 line of symmetry. It runs from the top vertex (between the two equal sides) straight down to the middle of the base, so the two equal sides fold onto each other.

workedExamples.title: State the order of rotational symmetry
workedExamples.prompt: What is the order of rotational symmetry of a rectangle that is not a square?
workedExamples.solution: Turn it around its centre. It looks the same after a half-turn (180°) and after a full turn (360°) — two matching positions. So the order is 2.

workedExamples.title: Will it tessellate?
workedExamples.prompt: Will regular hexagons tessellate? Show your reasoning with angles.
workedExamples.solution: Each angle of a regular hexagon is 120°. Three hexagons meet at a point: 3 × 120° = 360°, a full turn with no gap and no overlap. So yes, regular hexagons tessellate — just like a honeycomb.

workedExamples.title: Continue a pattern
workedExamples.prompt: A pattern goes: square, square, circle, square, square, circle … What is the 10th shape?
workedExamples.solution: The unit of repeat is ‘square, square, circle’ — a group of 3. The circles land at positions 3, 6, 9, 12 … The 10th shape is one after the 9th circle, so it is the first item of the next repeat: a square.

workedExamples.title: State the order of rotational symmetry of
workedExamples.prompt: State the order of rotational symmetry of: a) a square b) an equilateral triangle c) a rectangle (not a square).
workedExamples.solution: a) A square has rotational symmetry of order 4 (it matches itself every quarter-turn, 90°). b) An equilateral triangle has order 3 (it matches every third-of-a-turn, 120°). c) A rectangle that is not a square has order 2 (it matches after a half-turn, 180°, and a full turn).

workedExamples.title: Practice 10
workedExamples.prompt: Explain whether equilateral triangles tessellate, using the angle that meets at each point.
workedExamples.solution: Each angle of an equilateral triangle is 60°. Six of them meet at a point: 6 × 60° = 360°, a full turn with no gaps or overlaps. So yes, equilateral triangles tessellate.

workedExamples.title: Practice 11
workedExamples.prompt: In the pattern ●▲▲●▲▲●▲▲, what is the unit of repeat and what is the 9th shape?
workedExamples.solution: The unit of repeat is ●▲▲ (circle, triangle, triangle), 3 shapes long. Since 9 ÷ 3 = 3 exact repeats, the 9th shape is the last item of the repeat: ▲ (triangle).

workedExamples.title: Practice 12
workedExamples.prompt: A triangle is both isosceles and right-angled. State all three of its angles and explain your reasoning.
workedExamples.solution: The right angle is 90°; the other two must be equal (isosceles) and share the remaining 90°, so each is 45°. Angles: 90°, 45°, 45°.

activities.title: Shape Hunt
activities.materials: just your eyes, and paper to record what you find.
steps: Look around your home, the masjid, the market and your neighbourhood.
Find one example each of: a triangle, a square, a rectangle, a hexagon and a circle.
Sketch each one and label the shape name, the number of sides and the number of vertices.
For each triangle you find, decide whether it is equilateral, isosceles or scalene.
Keep your shape record – you can add to it all through this unit.

activities.title: Build Triangles with Sticks
activities.materials: straws, sticks, or dry stalks, cut to different lengths.
steps: Cut three sticks all the same length and build an equilateral triangle.
Cut two sticks the same and one different, and build an isosceles triangle.
Cut three sticks all different, and build a scalene triangle.
Push gently on each triangle. Notice how a triangle keeps its shape – this is why triangles are used in strong buildings.

activities.title: Paper-Folding Symmetry
steps: Fold a sheet of paper in half, then cut a shape along the folded edge.
Unfold it – the crease is a line of symmetry, and both halves match.
Try folding a square in four ways (two straight, two diagonal) to find all 4 lines of symmetry.
Now try a rectangle: which folds match and which do not? Explain why the diagonal folds fail.

activities.title: Make a Tessellation
steps: Cut out many identical squares, then many identical equilateral triangles.
Fit the squares together on a page with no gaps – you have made a tessellation.
Do the same with the triangles. How many meet at each point?
Now try to tessellate regular pentagons (cut several out). What goes wrong? Explain using the angles.

activities.title: Symmetry in Letters and Names (Investigation)
activities.materials: paper, a small mirror if you have one.
steps: Write the capital letters A, B, C, D, H, M, O, T, X, Y in large print.
Use the fold test (or the mirror) to find which letters have a line of symmetry, and how many.
Now write your own name in capitals and find the symmetry in each letter.
Which letters have rotational symmetry as well? (Hint: try H, O, X, S.)

activities.title: Design a Repeating Pattern (Family or Group Task)
activities.materials: coloured pencils or beads, and paper.
steps: Choose a unit of repeat using shapes and colours, for example ‘triangle-red, circle-blue’.
Repeat your unit across a border strip at least 12 items long.
Ask a family member (or your AI tutor if no one is available) to predict the 15th and 20th items using your rule.
Swap patterns with someone else and continue each other's designs.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand symmetry or tessellation best? What was the trickiest part? Which shapes surprised you? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Key rule 1
rules.text: Angle Sum Rules The three angles inside any triangle add up to 180 degrees. The four angles inside any quadrilateral add up to 360 degrees. To find a missing angle, add the ones you know and subtract from 180 (triangle) or 360 (quadrilateral).

rules.title: Key rule 2
rules.text: Symmetry Rules Line symmetry: fold along the line and both halves match exactly. Rotational symmetry order: how many times a shape looks the same in one full turn. Turn angle = 360 divided by the order of rotational symmetry.

rules.title: Tessellation Rule
rules.text: Shapes tessellate when the angles meeting at each point add up to exactly 360 degrees. Every triangle and every quadrilateral tessellates. Regular pentagons do not.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain, using angles, why regular hexagons tessellate but regular pentagons do not.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Regular hexagons have 120° angles and three meet at a point (3 × 120° = 360°), so they tessellate; regular pentagons have 108° angles, which does not divide into 360° (three give 324°, four give 432°), so they leave gaps or overlap.

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A parallelogram (that is not a rectangle or rhombus).

reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: With 4 shapes per repeat, the last shape lands on the multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12, 16, 20.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Line (Reflective) Symmetry.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
Symmetry is one of the most beautiful ideas in mathematics, and you can see it in flowers, in butterflies, in the patterns on a woven mat, and in the careful designs on a masjid door. A shape has line symmetry (also called reflective or mirror symmetry) when you can fold it along a straight line so that both halves match exactly, with one half sitting perfectly on top of the other. That fold line is called a line of symmetry.

The best way to test for a line of symmetry is the fold test: imagine folding the shape along the line. If the two halves land exactly on top of each other with no part sticking out, you have found a line of symmetry. It is like holding a mirror along the line – one half is the reflection of the other. Some shapes have no lines of symmetry, some have one, and some have many.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain the key idea in Rotational Symmetry.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer:
There is a second kind of symmetry that has nothing to do with folding. A shape has rotational symmetry if it looks exactly the same as you turn it around its centre point, before it has gone all the way round. Imagine pinning a shape at its centre and slowly spinning it: if at some point during a full turn it looks identical to how it started, it has rotational symmetry.

We measure rotational symmetry by its order – the number of times the shape looks the same during one complete turn (one full 360° rotation). To find the order, count how many different positions during a full turn look exactly like the starting position.

rounds.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a square have?

rounds.explanation: A square has 4 lines of symmetry: two through the midpoints of opposite sides and two along the diagonals.

rounds.prompt: A pentagon has 5 equal sides, but its angles are not all equal. Is it regular or irregular?
rounds.clue: Ask yourself what "Polygon" means here before you choose.
rounds.explanation: A polygon is only regular when ALL sides AND all angles are equal. Since the angles differ here, the shape is irregular even though its sides are equal.

rounds.prompt: Which of these shapes tessellates with no gaps or overlaps?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: Four squares meet at a point (4 × 90° = 360°), so squares tessellate perfectly; regular pentagons and octagons leave gaps, and circles cannot tile a flat surface at all.

rounds.prompt: A pattern repeats: triangle, circle, circle. What is the 8th shape?
rounds.clue: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
rounds.explanation: The unit of repeat is 3 shapes long (triangle, circle, circle). Since 8 = 3 × 2 + 2, the 8th shape is the 2nd item of the repeat, which is a circle.

selfAssessment: I can identify and name polygons by their number of sides, and tell regular from irregular polygons.
I can describe a shape using the correct language of sides, vertices (corners) and angles.
I can classify triangles by their sides (equilateral, isosceles, scalene) and by their angles (right, acute, obtuse).
I can classify quadrilaterals (square, rectangle, rhombus, parallelogram, trapezium, kite) by their properties.
I can find all the lines of symmetry in a 2D shape and understand line (reflective) symmetry.
I can understand rotational symmetry and state the order of rotational symmetry of a shape.
I can explain what a tessellation is and why some shapes tessellate while others leave gaps.
I can recognise, describe and continue repeating geometric patterns.
I can identify perpendicular lines (crossing at a right angle) and parallel lines (running in the same direction and never meeting) in shapes and in everyday objects.
I can create and complete patterns that have two lines of symmetry, such as a design reflected in both a vertical and a horizontal mirror line on a square grid.
